newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Canada to end blockade in salmon spat.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Canada to end blockade in salmon spat.

text.p: The United States on Monday urged Canadian authorities to enforce a court order to end a blockade of an Alaskan ferry by Canadian fisherman.

"The United States has protested and continues to protest this blockade," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "We also protest the refusal of Canadian federal authorities to stop the blockade or to enforce the court injunction. Canada must take action to enforce the court's judgment."

Canadian fishermen, angered by allegations that Alaskan fishermen were taking more than double their normal catch of salmon so far this year, continued their blockade of the Alaska state ferry Malaspina for a third day in the harbour at Prince Rupert, British Columbia, about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) north of Vancouver.

At the request of Alaska, a Canadian federal court on Sunday ordered the fishermen on Sunday to release the ship. But negotiations on ending the blockade collapsed and fishermen said new fishing boats and pleasure boats joined the siege on Monday.
"The Canadian government has not enforced that injunction, neither the provincial officials in British Columbia, nor the federal officials in Ottawa," Burns said.

"The blockade harms innocent people who have nothing to do with the salmon fishery," he said. "It also is unhelpful, very unhelpful, to our efforts, which we suppose and assume the government of Canada shares, to get the salmon talks back on track."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry urged an amicable end to the standoff, saying: "We hope it's peacefully resolved and the unnecessary hindrance that has been extended to the ferry passengers ends quickly."
Canada has accused the United States of overfishing Pacific Ocean salmon, while U.S. officials blame Canada for scuttling recent talks on how to divide this year's catch.
Canadian fisheries officials said that Alaskan fishermen have caught about three times more Canada-bound sockeye salmon so far this year than the average of previous years.
Burns said the increase in sockeye salmon caught this year was incidental to Alaskan catches of pink salmon, which the U.S. fishermen are entitled to take. The two species run together.
"The reason the totals are up is because the stock is more abundant this year," he said. "But the ratio of pink salmon to sockey salmon is consistent with ratios over the past couple of years."

Burns said it was time for the two sides to return to the negotiating table to resolve the dispute. They have held sporadic talks for months on how to divide Pacific salmon supplies but failed to reach an agreement before the start of this year's season.
Canada has asked for binding international arbitration to settle the dispute.

Burns said the United States would respond shortly to Canada's request. But he said Washington was concerned that binding arbitration would remove the process away from the people who would be most affected by the decision.

"We've always believed in the stakeholder process," Burns said. "Our people have been with us at these negotiations. We rely on the people of Washington (state) and Alaska to help us negotiate this. And we certainly want them to continue to participate."
